I review partner agreements for software companies, and the first thing I tell every sales director is this: do not read the contract from the first page to the last. Read it with two questions. What must we do, and what are we entitled to? Every clause answers one of those two questions. When you see the word shall, it is a duty. Invent shall pay the commission within thirty days. That is not a nice promise. It is an obligation, and if you do not do it, it is a breach. When you see is entitled to, it is a right. The partner is entitled to a commission. And when you see may, it is an option, something a party can do but does not have to do. The clause that people forget is termination. Everybody reads the commission. Nobody reads the notice period, and then one day they want to leave and discover that they have to wait ninety days.

I have signed partner agreements with eleven software vendors, and I read every one in the same order. First the territory, because a partner without a clear territory is just a reseller competing with the vendor's own sales team. Then exclusivity. I do not need exclusivity forever, but in the first two years I am going to invest in people and marketing, and I want to know that nobody else is selling the same product next door. Third, the commission, and when it is paid. Twenty per cent paid in thirty days is better than twenty-five paid in ninety. And last, liability. If the vendor's product fails, the vendor is liable. If the customer's own system fails, nobody should expect us to pay for it. When a vendor explains those four clauses to me in simple English on the first call, I usually sign. When the vendor sends the lawyer first, I usually do not.
